The Case for Abolishing the Supreme Court and Replacing Constitutional Interpretation with Democratic Principles

Introduction

The United States Supreme Court, once envisioned as a check against tyranny, has evolved into the most powerful unelected institution in modern American life—a body of nine lifetime appointees who wield practically unchecked authority over the meaning of the Constitution. Far from safeguarding liberty and equality, concentrated judicial power undermines democratic governance and causes deep social, political, and constitutional harm. The time has come to seriously consider replacing the current Supreme Court and judicial review with a system where constitutional meaning is determined through elected representatives and popular vote—placing constitutional authority back where the Founders first placed it: with the people and their representatives.

The Anti-Democratic Nature of Judicial Review

The Constitution does not explicitly grant judges the power of judicial review—the ability to overturn laws based on constitutional interpretation. Chief Justice John Marshall essentially invented this power in Marbury v. Madison (1803), giving unelected, lifetime-appointed judges a veto over the democratic process. This was never ratified by the people, approved by constitutional amendment, or endorsed by any democratic mandate.

The practical effect is stark: five unelected individuals can invalidate the will of millions of voters and their elected representatives. No other democracy on Earth grants judges comparable power. In Germany, Canada, South Africa, and elsewhere, constitutional courts operate within carefully designed frameworks—often with term limits, mandatory rotation, supermajority requirements for striking down laws, or systems that allow legislative override. The American system is an outlier precisely because it concentrates so much power in so few hands.

When the Supreme Court strikes down a law, it does so for all Americans—permanently and without recourse unless justices die, retire, or are persuaded to reverse themselves. A legislature that passes a law represents millions of voters. A Supreme Court that strikes it down represents five. The math of democracy doesn't add up.

Structural Harm to Democratic Governance

The harm caused by unchecked judicial power is not theoretical—it is structural, persistent, and deeply consequential.

Blocking popular reforms. Throughout history, the Court has repeatedly blocked legislation supported by substantial majorities. The Court struck down child labor laws, wage and price regulations, New Deal protections, and voting rights expansion. In Lochner v. New York (1905), the Court invented a "freedom of contract" doctrine from thin air to strike down worker protection laws—a philosophy so extreme that Court historians refer to the entire era as "the Lochner era" as a cautionary tale. Citizens United v. FEC (2010) constitutionalized unlimited corporate spending in elections—despite overwhelming public demand for campaign finance reform. In Shelby County v. Holder (2013), the Court gutted the Voting Rights Act, effectively ending preclearance requirements that had protected millions of minority voters for decades—all by a 5-4 vote.

In each case, a small number of appointed judges overruled the democratic process and entrenched their own policy preferences as constitutional law. The people had no vote. Their representatives had no override. The decision was final.

Political entrenchment and selection bias. Justices are appointed through an intensely political process and serve for life—an average of approximately 25-30 years per justice. The result is a system where presidents select justices largely based on ideology, and confirmation battles have become existential partisan warfare. The Court's legitimacy erodes with each openly political confirmation. When justices are selected primarily for political loyalty to presidential agendas, the idea that the Court serves as a neutral arbiter of law becomes impossible to sustain.

This is not a bug—it's a feature of the current system. Presidents choose justices knowing their policy impact will extend decades beyond any single administration. Justices staggered across generations lock in ideological configurations chosen by long-dead presidents onto living Americans. Today's Americans are governed in part by constitutional philosophies chosen for them without their input.

Punishing marginalized communities. The Court's record on race, gender, and civil rights is not one of consistent protection—it is one of profound missed opportunities and outright failures. Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857) declared Black people had "no rights which the white man was bound to respect." Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) enshrined "separate but equal" for six decades. For most of American history, the Court actively defended existing hierarchies against democratically driven efforts to dismantle them.

When the Court has advanced civil rights, it has often been in response to social movements that had already shifted public opinion—not ahead of them but behind them. Brown v. Board of Education (1954) came nearly 60 years after Plessy. Loving v. Virginia (1967), striking down bans on interracial marriage, came nearly a century after emancipation and after a majority of Americans had already shifted position. The Court led from behind, and only when social pressure made inaction untenable.

For millions of Americans, waiting for five justices to approve basic rights has meant waiting for justice that never came. Constitutions exist to protect minorities—but life-tenured jurists operating outside democratic accountability do not reliably serve that function.

Erosion of public trust and legitimacy. Trust in the Supreme Court has plummeted. Polling consistently shows declining public confidence—across partisan lines—driven by recognition that the Court operates as a political institution in judicial clothing. The confirmation crisis following Justice Scalia's death in 2016 (where the Senate refused to consider a nine-month-old vacancy) and the rushed confirmation of Justice Barrett in 2020 shattered any pretense of principled process. When the Court rules on deeply divisive issues—abortion, gun rights, religious liberty, healthcare—it is now widely perceived as reflecting the political preferences of a 5-4 or 6-3 majority rather than legal reasoning. This perception damages not just the Court but the broader democratic fabric, because citizens increasingly view constitutional law as politics by another name.

A Superior Alternative: Democratic Constitutional Interpretation

Abolishing the Supreme Court and replacing judicial review with democratic systems would not eliminate constitutional interpretation—it would relocate it to institutions that are accountable, transparent, and subject to popular will.

The alternative is not lawlessness. The alternative is democratic constitutionalism.

Elected representatives as constitutional interpreters. Under this system, Congress would exercise primary authority to interpret the Constitution's application to legislation. When passing laws, Congress would explicitly articulate the constitutional basis for each piece of legislation, subject to internal debate, committee review, and floor debate. This already happens in a diluted form—Congress routinely debates constitutional questions—but it would become the authoritative interpretive mechanism.

This approach has clear democratic advantages. If voters disagree with their representative's constitutional interpretation, they can vote them out. Constitutional meaning becomes responsive to evolving public understanding rather than locked into the philosophies of justices appointed decades earlier. When constitutional questions become contested, the resolution occurs through democratic deliberation—the mechanism the Constitution itself establishes for resolving fundamental questions.

The concern that legislatures would ignore the Constitution misunderstands the proposal. Congress would still be bound by constitutional text. The change is in enforcement mechanism: rather than having five appointed judges as final arbiter, constitutional questions would be resolved through legislative process, with the backstop of judicial review at lower courts that can identify constitutional questions for legislative attention.

Popular vote and referenda for fundamental constitutional questions. For the most consequential constitutional questions—those affecting fundamental rights or structural changes—a national referendum mechanism could be established through constitutional amendment. This would allow the American people to directly decide contested constitutional questions, rather than delegating those decisions to nine legal scholars.

The Swiss system demonstrates this is workable: the Swiss Confederation regularly puts fundamental rights questions to popular vote and has developed robust traditions of direct democratic constitutional decisionmaking. The Nordic countries, the United Kingdom's approach to human rights (where Parliament can override judicial declarations of incompatibility), and South Africa's constitutional system all demonstrate that strong rights protections can coexist with democratic constitutional authority.

A national referendum system would require constitutional amendment—but that itself demonstrates the point. The highest form of democratic expression would control the highest questions of constitutional meaning.

Maintaining appellate courts without Supreme Court supremacy. Lower federal courts and even an appellate court could continue to play a role in identifying constitutional questions, interpreting statutory consistency, and flagging potential constitutional concerns to Congress through advisory opinions. But the final authority to determine constitutional meaning would rest with democratic institutions—not with life-tenured appointees.

This preserves legal expertise and eliminates the red herring that the alternative to judicial supremacy is legal chaos. It simply relocates final interpretive authority to accountable institutions.

Addressing Concerns

The "tyranny of the majority" objection. Critics will argue that removing judicial review abandons minorities to majority will. This objection deserves serious engagement—but it ultimately fails, for several reasons.

First, it assumes the Supreme Court reliably protects minorities—which, as shown above, history does not support. The Court defended slavery, segregation, gender discrimination, corporate exploitation, and voter suppression for most of American history. The notion that the Court is a consistent guardian of minority rights is based on the exceptional mid-20th century period, not on its historical record.

Second, elected representatives already protect minority interests through political coalitions, interest group advocacy, and electoral competition. The success of the abolitionist movement, women's suffrage, labor organizing, and LGBTQ rights all progressed primarily through democratic mobilization—not judicial grant. Judicial victories like Brown and Obergefell codified changes already underway in public opinion rather than creating them from nothing.

Third, the "tyranny" concern is addressed by retaining constitutional text as binding law. Elected representatives would still operate within constitutional constraints—they simply wouldn't have five appointed judges claiming a monopoly on constitutional meaning. The First Amendment would still prohibit Congress from establishing religion or restricting free speech; the Fourteenth Amendment would still require equal protection. The difference is that democratic processes—not judicial fiat—would determine how these principles apply to specific questions.

Fourth, and most fundamentally: the answer to democratic failure is more democracy, not less. If a democratic majority pursues unjust policies, the solution is organizing, persuasion, voter engagement, and political action—the tools citizens actually control. The solution is not hoping that Justices Thomas and Alito come around to your position.

The "rule of law" concern. Critics will argue that removing the Court undermines the rule of law. This conflates two distinct concepts: (1) the rule of law as general principle that government is bound by legal rules, and (2) judicial supremacy as the specific institutional arrangement of judges having final constitutional authority. The former does not require the latter.

Government would still operate under constitutional text. Congress would still be bound by explicit constitutional prohibitions. Legal systems without judicial supremacy—including the UK, Netherlands, Norway, and Switzerland—maintain robust rule of law traditions. The rule of law does not require nine people in robes to have the final word.

The "legal expertise" concern. Critics will argue that judges possess specialized constitutional expertise that legislators lack. This is true—and it is exactly why lower courts and judicial advisors would continue to analyze constitutional questions and flag concerns for legislative consideration. Expertise informs democratic decisionmaking; it does not replace it.

Moreover, the assumption that constitutional law expertise produces better outcomes is questionable. Constitutional law is not physics—it is contested moral and political philosophy. Reasonable people profoundly disagree about whether the Fourteenth Amendment concept of "liberty" encompasses a right to abortion, whether the Second Amendment protects an individual gun right unconnected to militia service, or whether the Equal Protection Clause prohibits affirmative action. In these disputes, democratic deliberation through accountable institutions produces outcomes more legitimate than the opinions of five lawyers.

Historical and Comparative Support

The proposal aligns deeply with American constitutional history. The Constitution itself places sovereignty in "We the People"—not in judicial hierarchies. The Declaration of Independence derives governmental legitimacy from the consent of the governed—a principle that applies to institutions claiming to govern in the people's name.

Comparative democracy consistently supports democratic constitutional systems. The United Kingdom has long operated without powerful judicial review and developed strong rights protections through parliamentary process. The Nordic countries, among the world's most free and equal societies, do not vest constitutional authority in supreme courts as the United States does. Switzerland's system of direct democratic constitutional referenda has protected liberty, equality, and prosperity for generations.

America's outlier status is not a strength—it is a historical accident with increasingly harmful consequences.

Conclusion

The case for abolishing the Supreme Court and replacing judicial review with democratic constitutional interpretation is not radical—it is a restoration of foundational American principles. The Constitution begins with "We the People." It establishes legislative, executive, and judicial branches of government, each deriving authority from the people. It does not establish a judicial aristocracy with the power to overrule the democratic process permanently and without recourse.

What the Supreme Court has become—nunelected, life-tenured, politically selected, practically unreviewable—is a feature the Founders never designed and most of them would have found alarming. Alexander Hamilton, who in Federalist No. 78 described the judiciary as the "least dangerous branch," would scarcely recognize today's Court: it has become simultaneously the most powerful, most politically consequential, and least accountable institution in American governance.

Democratic constitutionalism—constitutional interpretation determined by elected representatives and, for the most fundamental questions, by the people themselves—would not produce perfect outcomes. But it would produce legitimate outcomes. It would restore constitutional authority to its rightful owners. It would align institutional power with democratic accountability. And it would finally honor the opening words of the Constitution that American democracy supposedly rests upon: "We the People."

The question is not whether democratic self-governance is risky—it is. But concentrating power in nine unelected officials has proven far more dangerous. The Supreme Court's unchecked authority has blocked popular reforms, entrenched political minorities, undermined faith in government, and failed the very minorities it claims to protect. It is time to put constitutional authority back where it belongs: in the hands of those who must answer to the people.

Abolishing the U.S. Supreme Court and ending strong-form judicial review is a minority view, but it has a serious intellectual tradition. Supporters of this idea generally want constitutional questions decided more directly by democratic institutions and the public, rather than by a small group of life-tenured judges.

Below is a neutral summary of the main reasons they give and the supposed benefits they claim would follow, along with the kinds of democratic mechanisms they envision as replacements.

1. Background: What’s being challenged?

Two core features are targeted:

  1. The U.S. Supreme Court as final arbiter of the Constitution
    In practice, the Court has the last word on the constitutionality of federal and state laws, executive actions, and many public policies.

  2. Judicial review in its “strong-form” U.S. version
    The Court can invalidate laws and policies with binding effect; changing its interpretation generally requires either:

    • A constitutional amendment (very hard to pass), or
    • A later Court reversing itself (unpredictable and politicized).

Critics want to replace this with democratic mechanisms where elected bodies or the people themselves have primary responsibility for interpreting and enforcing constitutional norms.

2. Democratic legitimacy and the “countermajoritarian” problem

A central objection is that strong judicial review is undemocratic.

2.1 Unelected, life-tenured judges

Proponents of abolition argue:

  • Supreme Court justices are not elected and serve life terms, yet they make far-reaching decisions about rights, elections, social policy, and economic regulation.
  • This gives immense power to a tiny group that can override legislation enacted by officials who are directly accountable to voters.
  • In a system that claims to rest on government “by the people,” it is odd to give the final word on foundational questions to a body that is largely insulated from public control.

This is often called the “countermajoritarian difficulty”: the Court can nullify the expressed will of electoral majorities (or even supermajorities).

2.2 Democratic self-government and “who should decide?”

On this view, a democracy should allow citizens, through their representatives, to:

  • Debate rights and constitutional principles,
  • Make collective decisions about contested moral issues,
  • And correct mistakes through elections and legislation.

Judicial supremacy is seen as short-circuiting democratic deliberation, moving major moral and political questions from the public sphere to legal elites.

3. The Court as a political, not neutral, institution

Proponents of abolition argue that the Supreme Court is inherently political, despite the rhetoric of neutrality and legal expertise.

3.1 Ideological appointments and partisan alignment

Common points:

  • Justices are nominated and confirmed through an overtly partisan process, and voting patterns on the Court often align predictably with political ideology.
  • Major decisions—on voting rights, campaign finance, abortion, labor, and more—frequently track the preferences of the party that appointed the majority of justices.
  • This undermines the claim that the Court is a neutral, technical interpreter of law rather than a “super-legislature” pursuing policy goals.

From this angle, abolitionists say: if decisions will inevitably reflect values and ideology, those choices should be made by elected politicians who can be removed from office, not life-tenured judges.

3.2 Judicial supremacy and shrinking of politics

Some scholars argue that when courts have the last word on constitutional meaning:

  • Political actors begin to frame disputes as legal questions, hoping for victories in court instead of building broad popular support.
  • Citizens may become more passive, seeing rights and constitutional change as “lawyers’ business,” not their own responsibility.
  • Constitutional politics is displaced from legislatures, parties, and movements to litigation.

By removing or sharply reducing judicial supremacy, supporters hope to re-center constitutional debate in the democratic arena, increasing political responsibility and civic engagement.

4. Mixed historical record on rights and justice

A key empirical argument is that the Supreme Court has not consistently protected rights or minorities, and that its overall record is at best mixed.

4.1 Famous failures

Critics point to historical decisions such as:

  • Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857) – denying citizenship and rights to Black people, effectively entrenching slavery.
  • Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) – upholding racial segregation.
  • Korematsu v. United States (1944) – endorsing internment of Japanese Americans.
  • Decisions weakening labor protections and upholding harsh economic inequalities in the early 20th century.
  • More recent decisions critiqued for restricting voting rights or expanding corporate political influence.

From this perspective:

  • The Court has often validated oppressive regimes and resisted egalitarian reforms.
  • It tends to be conservative in the small-c sense: protective of existing power structures, cautious about social change, and slow to recognize new rights claims.

4.2 Democratic systems can protect rights without strong judicial review

Abolitionists often argue that:

  • Many established democracies (e.g., the UK, New Zealand, some Nordic countries) have historically had weaker forms of judicial review or parliamentary supremacy, yet still maintain robust rights protections.
  • Rights protections often come from strong political cultures, active civil society, independent media, and electoral accountability, not just from courts.

The claim is that good democratic design and political practice can protect rights at least as well as, and sometimes better than, a powerful constitutional court.

5. Structural and institutional concerns

5.1 Centralization of constitutional authority

Having one court with near-final authority:

  • Centralizes constitutional interpretation in Washington, D.C.
  • Reduces space for local experimentation or diverse regional understandings.
  • Encourages strategic litigation to secure nationwide rulings, sometimes bypassing gradual democratic debate.

Abolition or serious reduction of judicial review is seen as a way to decentralize constitutional meaning, letting different institutions and communities reason through issues in parallel.

5.2 Veto point and status quo bias

Judicial review functions as an additional veto point in the political system:

  • New policies can be blocked even when they have strong popular and legislative support.
  • This tends to favor the status quo and those who benefit from existing arrangements.
  • Well-resourced actors (corporations, wealthy interests) may have greater ability to litigate and use courts to defend their prerogatives.

From this standpoint, eliminating the Court’s power to strike down legislation can make democratic systems more responsive and less skewed toward entrenched interests.

6. Supposed benefits of abolition or drastic curtailment

Proponents argue that abolishing the Supreme Court (or converting it into a non-supreme, non-constitutional court) and ending strong-form judicial review would bring several benefits.

6.1 Stronger democratic accountability

  • Constitutional decisions would be made primarily by elected bodies (Congress, state legislatures, executive officials).
  • Citizens could respond to constitutional interpretations they dislike through elections, rather than waiting for judicial appointments to shift the Court’s composition.
  • This would make constitutional development more visibly tied to popular will.

6.2 Greater public ownership of the Constitution

  • Without a supreme judicial arbiter, constitutional meaning becomes a matter of public debate and political contestation.
  • Citizens, movements, and parties would be more likely to:
    • Invoke constitutional principles in campaigns,
    • Propose constitutional reforms directly,
    • Treat the Constitution as a “living political document” rather than a specialized legal code.

This is sometimes called “popular constitutionalism”: the idea that the people themselves, not the courts, are the primary interpreters of the Constitution.

6.3 More flexible and adaptive constitutional development

With fewer judicial barriers:

  • Legislatures could experiment with different approaches to complex issues (e.g., campaign finance rules, social welfare policies, labor protections).
  • Political communities could adjust constitutional norms more rapidly as values and conditions change, rather than waiting for decades of litigation or difficult formal amendments.
  • Constitutional interpretation would evolve through ongoing legislative practice and political negotiation.

6.4 Reduced politicization around judicial appointments

  • If the Supreme Court no longer had the final say over major constitutional questions—or if it were abolished:
    • The stakes of judicial appointments would fall.
    • Confirmation battles might become less polarized and less central to national politics.
  • The fierce, high-stakes struggles over a handful of seats would be replaced by more routine political battles over elections and legislation.

6.5 Less legal complexity as a barrier to justice

  • A system less dominated by constitutional litigation may:
    • Reduce the need for highly specialized and expensive legal advocacy to secure rights.
    • Make rights claims more accessible through political organizing and legislative advocacy, which some see as more egalitarian avenues than the courts.

In this picture, politics—not litigation—becomes the main arena for advancing justice and rights.

7. Democratic mechanisms proposed as replacements

Those who want to abolish or sharply limit the Supreme Court’s power typically do not want to abandon constitutionalism. They propose alternative democratic mechanisms for interpreting and enforcing the Constitution.

Different proposals include:

7.1 Legislative supremacy

  • Congress and state legislatures would have the final word on what laws the Constitution permits, subject only to:
    • Elections, and
    • Constitutional amendments passed through democratic procedures.
  • Courts (if they exist) would apply statutes but would not strike them down as unconstitutional.

Variations might include:

  • Requiring supermajority votes in legislatures for laws that limit certain rights.
  • Specialized constitutional committees within legislatures to scrutinize bills for consistency with constitutional principles.

7.2 Popular constitutionalism and referenda

Some proposals emphasize direct citizen involvement:

  • National or state referenda on major constitutional questions (e.g., voting rights rules, campaign finance, reproductive rights).
  • Periodic constitutional conventions or citizen assemblies where randomly selected or elected citizens deliberate on reforms and submit proposals to the public.

Here, the people themselves act as the ultimate constitutional court.

7.3 Weak-form review and legislative overrides

Even critics of strong review sometimes allow limited judicial roles:

  • Courts can interpret the Constitution and issue opinions that a law is incompatible with rights, but cannot invalidate it.
    • Legislatures then decide whether to change the law in response.
  • Or, courts can strike down laws, but legislatures can override those decisions by:
    • A simple or supermajority vote,
    • Possibly with additional democratic safeguards (e.g., two successive legislatures).

This retains judicial input but ensures that elected bodies have the final say.

7.4 Independent democratic bodies for rights protection

Instead of a supreme court, some suggest:

  • Human rights commissions, ombudsman offices, or equality bodies with investigative and advisory powers.
  • These institutions can:
    • Monitor rights compliance,
    • Publicly report on violations,
    • Recommend changes,
    • But not unilaterally veto laws.

They would rely on public pressure and political accountability rather than judicial coercion.

7.5 Constitutional amendment reforms

To make democratic constitutionalism workable, abolitionists often pair their proposals with changes to the amendment process:

  • Lower thresholds for amendments (e.g., less rigid than the current Article V process).
  • Requiring multiple popular votes over time or ratification by broadly representative assemblies, to balance flexibility with stability.
  • Regularly scheduled opportunities for constitutional revision, ensuring that constitutional change is an ongoing democratic process.

8. Overall rationale, in summary

Those who want to abolish the U.S. Supreme Court and strong judicial review generally believe:

  • Constitutional interpretation is unavoidably political and value-laden.
  • Therefore, it ought to be handled by institutions that are directly accountable to the people, not by life-tenured judges.
  • The Court’s historical and contemporary record shows that it is not a consistently reliable guardian of rights or democracy.
  • Democracies can protect rights and manage deep disagreements through political institutions, public deliberation, and robust democratic culture, rather than relying on judicial supremacy.

In their view, shifting constitutional authority from courts to democratic mechanisms would:

  • Increase democratic legitimacy,
  • Encourage citizen engagement with constitutional questions,
  • Reduce elite domination of constitutional meaning,
  • And make the constitutional order more responsive and adaptable.

Others strongly dispute these claims and defend the Court and judicial review; this answer has focused on explaining the arguments of those who favor abolition or drastic reduction of judicial power.

Friends, neighbors, fellow citizens,

We are told, from grade school onward, that the United States Supreme Court is the “guardian of the Constitution”—the final word on right and wrong, on liberty and power, on what we may and may not do as a free people.

But let’s say out loud what too few dare to say:
No free people should surrender their deepest constitutional decisions to nine unelected, unaccountable lawyers in black robes.

It is time—past time—to abolish the Supreme Court as we know it and to end the power of judicial review. Constitutional questions belong to the people and their elected representatives, not to a tiny, insulated judicial elite.

A Republic Ruled by Nine

We live in a nation of more than 330 million people. We elect thousands of representatives: city councilors, state legislators, governors, members of Congress, a president. We debate, we vote, we argue, we compromise. That is democracy. That is republican self-government.

And then, after all of that, nine individuals—appointed for life, never subjected to a popular vote, often chosen decades ago—can erase the work, the will, and the wisdom of an entire nation with the stroke of a pen.

One decision. Five votes out of nine.
Five human beings can overrule:

  • Unanimous votes of legislatures,
  • Massive public majorities,
  • Decades of democratic practice.

We are told this is “checks and balances.” But what do you call it when the check has no balance? When the guardians guard only themselves? When the people, in whose name the Constitution exists, have no direct say?

We call it what it is: rule by a judicial oligarchy.

Judicial Review Is Not Sacred

We are taught that “this is how it has to be.” But that is not true.

The power of judicial review—the idea that the Supreme Court may strike down laws as “unconstitutional” and that its word is final—is not written in the text of the Constitution. It was asserted by the Court itself in Marbury v. Madison in 1803.

Think about that.
The Court claimed for itself the power to invalidate the acts of the elected branches—and we simply accepted it as fate.

No democratic vote.
No constitutional amendment.
Just nine judges saying, in effect: “We will decide.”

Other democracies do not give such sweeping, unchecked power to judges. Many have constitutional courts that can be overridden by popular will or legislative supermajorities. Some allow referenda to settle constitutional questions. Some provide for frequent constitutional revision by elected representatives.

We, by contrast, act as though a handful of lifetime appointees must be infallible, as though democracy is somehow too dangerous to be trusted with its own Constitution.

That is not self-government.
That is a soft, legalistic monarchy.

When Rights Are Held Hostage

Defenders of judicial supremacy will say, “But the Court protects our rights from the tyranny of the majority.” That sounds noble. But in practice, it means something far more troubling:

Our rights exist only if five justices agree.

Your bodily autonomy, your voting rights, your ability to marry who you love, your right to organize, to speak, to protest, to be free from arbitrary police power—all of it, under judicial supremacy, lives or dies based on the personal philosophy of a tiny group of people you never chose.

And that power swings wildly with each new appointment:

  • One generation’s Court upholds segregation; another strikes it down.
  • One Court shreds voting protections; another might restore them.
  • One Court expands corporate power; another might cut it back.

Are those really “constitutional principles”? Or are we watching, decade after decade, a battle of ideologies disguised as neutral law?

When we let nine justices define the meaning of our rights, we are not protected from politics—we are ruled by it. The difference is that their politics are unaccountable, irreversible, and shielded from direct public judgment.

If a legislature violates your rights, you can vote them out.
If a president tramples your freedoms, you can organize, protest, and defeat them at the ballot box.

But when the Supreme Court does these things, you are told:
“Nothing can be done. Respect the decision. Wait a generation.”

That is not freedom. That is resignation.

Democracy Is Not the Enemy of the Constitution

We must reject the poisonous idea that the people cannot be trusted with their own fundamental law. The Constitution was not written to chain us to the past. It was written to establish a framework of self-rule—to be interpreted, applied, and, when necessary, changed by the living, breathing nation it governs.

Who should decide what the Constitution means in our time?

  • The people who live under it.
  • The representatives we elect and can remove.
  • The communities that will bear the consequences.

Constitutional questions should be answered democratically—through:

  • Legislation at the state and federal level,
  • Constitutional amendments and conventions,
  • Popular referenda and citizen assemblies,
  • Transparent, accountable processes where the people are not spectators, but protagonists.

This does not mean rights disappear. It means rights are grounded in living democratic consensus, not in the shifting composition of a distant bench.

“But What About Minority Rights?”

Some will say, “If you get rid of judicial review, what protects minorities?” That is the hardest, and most important, question.

Here is the honest answer: no nine people can guarantee justice for minorities in a society that does not care. Real protection for vulnerable groups has never come primarily from benevolent judges. It has come from:

  • Organizing,
  • Protest,
  • Moral argument,
  • Political struggle,
  • Changing the hearts and minds of the majority.

Courts often lag behind social movements, and sometimes stand in the way. They upheld slavery, segregation, Japanese internment, mass surveillance, bans on labor organizing. They have repeatedly failed the very people we are told they uniquely protect.

Minority rights are safer when:

  • Communities are mobilized,
  • Laws reflect real, broad-based commitments,
  • Constitutional principles are debated out in the open, not whispered in elite chambers.

Democracy is messy. It is imperfect. It can be unjust. But the answer to imperfect democracy is more democracy—deeper participation, stronger protections written by representatives we control—not the elevation of an untouchable legal priesthood.

A Court Above the Law

We demand transparency from agencies, ethics from public servants, accountability from our elected officials. Yet the Supreme Court—the most powerful institution in our constitutional system in many respects—operates behind closed doors, bound by its own vague ethical standards, insulated from real consequences.

  • Justices are appointed for life, regardless of changing public values.
  • They can refuse to recuse themselves from glaring conflicts of interest.
  • They can overturn long-settled precedents with a bare majority.
  • They face no direct mechanism of recall or popular censure.

This is not normal. It would be unthinkable in any other branch of government. Why have we accepted it here?

Because we have been taught to revere the Court as something above politics, above error, above the people. Yet the record of history is clear: the Court is not above politics—it is steeped in it. It is not above error—it has committed some of the gravest wrongs in our national story.

No institution should hold this much power without democratic accountability.

Abolishing the Supreme Court as we know it and ending judicial review does not mean plunging into chaos. It means redesigning our system so that constitutional authority flows from where it was always meant to flow: the people.

What might that look like?

  • Eliminate the Court’s power of final judicial review.
    Courts can interpret law in individual cases, but may not strike down democratically enacted statutes as “unconstitutional” with binding authority over the entire nation.

  • Return constitutional interpretation to elected branches.
    Let Congress and state legislatures bear the responsibility for determining constitutional meaning in their laws and policies, subject to direct political accountability.

  • Create democratic mechanisms for constitutional change.
    Make it easier to amend the Constitution through supermajority votes, conventions, or popular referenda, so that the people can adapt their fundamental law without waiting for judicial permission.

  • Establish alternative advisory bodies if needed.
    Constitutional councils, citizen assemblies, or expert commissions could offer non-binding interpretations to inform legislative debate—guidance, not rule.

These reforms would not weaken the Constitution. They would root it where it belongs: in the people’s ongoing, contested, living judgment.

A Call to Courage

To take this step is to admit something hard: we have been wrong to worship the Court. We have mistaken judicial power for constitutional fidelity. We have entangled our hopes for justice with the decisions of a few distant strangers.

It is time to grow up as a republic.

A mature democracy does not outsource its conscience. It does not say, “We cannot be trusted with our own freedom; let others decide for us.” It accepts responsibility. It takes on the hard work of argument, persuasion, and compromise.

We must demand:

  • Constitutional amendments that strip the Supreme Court of its supremacy,
  • Public campaigns that expose the myth of judicial infallibility,
  • Movements that insist our fundamental rights be secured by democratic will, not judicial grace.

This will not be easy. Those who benefit from judicial supremacy will call this idea radical, dangerous, even heretical. But ask yourself:

What is more dangerous—trusting the people with their own Constitution, or entrusting it forever to a small, unaccountable elite?

What is more radical—extending democratic self-government to the highest questions of law, or preserving a system where five individuals can rule over hundreds of millions?

What is more faithful to the spirit of 1776—the quiet acceptance of judicial monarchy, or the bold insistence that no authority stands above the people?

Take Back What Is Yours

The Constitution begins with three words: “We the People.” Not “We the Judges.” Not “We the Lawyers.” Not “We the Appointed Few.”

For too long, we have allowed those words to become a ritual incantation, not a governing reality. To abolish the Supreme Court’s rule and end judicial review is to take those words seriously—terribly, wonderfully, demanding-ly seriously.

It is to say:

  • We will not be ruled by nine.
  • We will not accept that our most basic rights hang on one swing vote.
  • We will not abandon our responsibility to decide, together, what justice requires.

Let us reclaim our Constitution from the marble temple and return it to its rightful home: in our debates, our elections, our assemblies, our communities, our hands.

The path forward is clear:

Organize. Educate. Demand amendments. Elect representatives who will fight to dismantle judicial supremacy. Build a movement that insists that the last word on our Constitution does not belong to a court—it belongs to us.

Not someday. Not in some abstract future.

Now.

Because a free people does not wait patiently for permission to govern itself. A free people stands up and says:

Our rights are ours to define.
Our laws are ours to shape.
Our Constitution is ours to interpret.

And our future will never again be decided by nine.

Abolish the Supreme Court: Restoring Democratic Sovereignty by Eliminating Judicial Review

In the summer of 1787, the framers of the United States Constitution crafted a document designed to balance governmental powers and protect individual liberty. Among the three branches they established, the judiciary was deliberately conceived as the “least dangerous” to the political rights of the Constitution, lacking both the power of the sword and the purse. Chief Justice John Marshall, writing in Marbury v. Madison (1803), however, single-handedly expanded this weak branch into a towering arbiter of American life by asserting the power of judicial review – the authority to invalidate laws passed by the people’s elected representatives. This power, nowhere explicitly granted by the Constitution, has since allowed nine unelected judges to override the will of millions, shaping policy on pivotal issues from campaign finance to reproductive rights. It is high time to correct this constitutional aberration by abolishing the Supreme Court as we know it, eliminating judicial review, and returning the authority to interpret the Constitution to elected representatives or the people themselves through direct democracy. This essay argues that such a radical shift is necessary to restore democratic legitimacy, ensure governmental accountability, and protect the core principle of popular sovereignty.

The foremost reason to abolish the Supreme Court and judicial review is their fundamentally undemocratic character. The United States was founded on the creed that governments derive “their just powers from the consent of the governed.” Yet, the Supreme Court Justices are appointed for life, without any direct electoral mandate, and are virtually immune to public accountability. No election, no recall, and no popular vote can remove a Justice whose decisions may profoundly affect the lives of citizens. This insulation from public opinion is often defended as a guard against the tyranny of the majority, but it also creates a significant democratic deficit. When nine unelected individuals can overturn laws enacted by the people’s representatives, they are effectively ruling without the consent of the governed. In a true democracy, the ultimate authority to make binding decisions should rest with those who are answerable to the electorate. The notion that a small, elite cadre of judges can have the final say on matters of public policy contradicts the most basic tenet of democratic governance.

The historical context of judicial review reveals that it is not a legitimate constitutional principle but an act of judicial usurpation. The framers, including Thomas Jefferson and James Madison, expressed deep reservations about the power of courts to annul legislation. Jefferson famously warned that “the judiciary is the most dangerous branch because it is the weakest and least accountable,” and he feared that judges would use their interpretations to impose their own policy preferences. Indeed, the Constitution itself contains no explicit grant of judicial review; it was a power the Court simply assumed for itself in Marbury. This self-appointed authority has allowed the judiciary to transform from a minor branch into the ultimate check on the other two, upsetting the delicate balance the framers intended. The legitimacy of judicial review rests on a legal fiction – that the Constitution is a “law” that judges apply – but in reality, it is a political document whose meaning is inherently contested and must be resolved through democratic processes.

The Supreme Court’s track record is littered with decisions that expose its inability to serve as a neutral guardian of rights and its susceptibility to the prevailing prejudices of the time. Consider Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857), which denied citizenship to African Americans and declared that Congress could not prohibit slavery in the territories. Or Plessy v. Ferguson (1896), which upheld racial segregation under the “separate but equal” doctrine. More recent examples include Korematsu v. United States (1944), which sanctioned the internment of Japanese Americans, and Citizens United v. FEC (2010), which opened the floodgates for corporate money in elections. Even the Court’s occasional forays into protecting minority rights, such as Brown v. Board of Education (1954), were deeply controversial and did little to alter the underlying reality that the Court’s composition changes with the political winds, leading to inconsistent and unpredictable jurisprudence. Indeed, the overturning of Roe v. Wade (1973) in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization (2022) demonstrates how constitutional “rights” can evaporate simply because the Court’s ideological balance shifted. This instability undermines the rule of law and erodes public confidence in the judiciary as an impartial institution.

The myth of judicial expertise and neutrality is easily dispelled upon closer examination. Constitutional interpretation is not a purely technical exercise; it is an inherently political and value-laden endeavor that requires making choices among competing visions of the Constitution’s meaning. The Supreme Court’s decisions are rarely unanimous; they often split along ideological lines that correspond closely to the appointing president’s party affiliation. The process of selecting Justices has become a high-stakes political battle, with nominees grilled about their views on hot-button issues. If the Court’s role were truly apolitical, such battles would be unnecessary. Instead, we witness the Court becoming a focal point for partisan warfare, with each side hoping to capture the Court to advance its agenda. This politicization corrupts the Court’s legitimacy and encourages a cynical view of the Constitution as a tool for judicial activism rather than a framework for democratic self-governance.

Rejecting judicial review does not mean abandoning a written Constitution or sacrificing the protection of rights. Rather, it means entrusting constitutional interpretation to the institutions that are most accountable to the people. Many successful democracies operate without judicial review or with a much weaker version. The United Kingdom, for instance, adheres to the principle of parliamentary sovereignty, whereby Parliament is the supreme lawmaker and its statutes cannot be invalidated by courts. Canada’s Charter of Rights and Freedoms includes a “notwithstanding clause” that allows legislatures to override certain judicial decisions. In Switzerland, constitutional amendments are regularly approved by popular referendum, giving the people direct authority over the fundamental law. These systems demonstrate that constitutional interpretation can be managed through democratic processes without relying on an unaccountable judiciary.

In the American context, we could establish a system where constitutional questions are resolved by Congress with a supermajority requirement (e.g., two-thirds of both houses) or by a national referendum called upon the petition of a certain number of citizens. Such a system would ensure that constitutional interpretations reflect a broad national consensus rather than the views of a few appointed judges. It would also encourage more thoughtful and inclusive public deliberation about the meaning of our fundamental law, as the people and their representatives would need to engage directly with constitutional issues rather than leaving them to “expert” judges. The process could be designed to protect minority rights by requiring heightened majorities, thus ensuring that constitutional changes are not made lightly but also that they are ultimately subject to democratic control.

Critics contend that eliminating judicial review would leave minority rights vulnerable to majoritarian tyranny. Yet, history shows that the Supreme Court itself has often been the oppressor rather than the protector of minorities. The Court’s decisions in Dred Scott, Plessy, and Korematsu are stark reminders that an unelected judiciary can and does endorse systemic discrimination when the prevailing political climate demands it. Moreover, rights are more securely protected when they are rooted in the lived experience and evolving moral consensus of the people, not in the abstract reasoning of isolated judges. In a system where elected bodies interpret the Constitution, minority groups would have a direct voice in the political process – through lobbying, voting, and public advocacy – to influence constitutional meanings. This is preferable to relying on the unpredictable benevolence of nine lawyers. Additionally, a more explicit and carefully drafted Bill of Rights, with protections that are difficult to amend but not immune to democratic revision, could serve as a robust shield for individual liberties while still preserving popular sovereignty.

The transition away from judicial review and the Supreme Court can be achieved through a constitutional amendment, the most legitimate method of altering the fundamental law. Such an amendment could explicitly strip the Supreme Court of the power of judicial review, transferring that authority to Congress with procedural safeguards, such as a two-thirds vote or a concurrent resolution of both houses. Alternatively, the amendment could establish a Constitutional Council composed of elected officials or a mixed body of judges and legislators, but with the crucial difference that its members would be removable by the electorate or subject to term limits. Another approach would be to grant Congress the power to override any Supreme Court decision by a supermajority, effectively making the Court’s interpretations advisory rather than binding. While the amendment process is deliberately difficult, the growing dissatisfaction with the Court’s politicization may create the necessary momentum for change.

In conclusion, the abolition of the Supreme Court and the elimination of judicial review are not radical ideas for the sake of disruption; they are necessary steps to restore the United States to its foundational principle of government by the people. The current system concentrates too much power in an unelected, unaccountable body that has repeatedly demonstrated its fallibility and susceptibility to political bias. By vesting constitutional interpretation in elected representatives or in the people directly, we can ensure that our fundamental law evolves with contemporary values, that decisions are made through transparent democratic processes, and that the voices of all citizens are heard. The framers feared a powerful judiciary; we must act to realize their fears by dismantling the very institution they warned could become a threat to liberty and democracy. The time has come to reclaim the Constitution for the people.

Introduction

  • Adaptability
    Legislative or referendum-based interpretation can evolve more quickly in response to changing societal values and new challenges, without waiting for litigation to reach the courts or for constitutional amendments.

Introduction

The United States Supreme Court, long revered as the ultimate guardian of constitutional principles, has evolved into an undemocratic super-legislature that undermines the very foundations of popular sovereignty upon which this nation was built. The Democratic Deficit of Judicial Supremacy

Unaccountable Power

The current system grants extraordinary power to individuals who face no electoral accountability. Supreme Court justices, appointed for life, routinely overturn laws passed by democratically elected representatives, effectively legislating from the bench without any mechanism for the people to register their disapproval. When five justices can invalidate legislation supported by hundreds of elected officials and millions of voters, we witness not the protection of rights but the subversion of democracy itself.

This creates a temporal democratic deficit where the political preferences of past electoral minorities govern present majorities—a fundamental violation of democratic principles.

The Mythology of Legal Objectivity

The notion that judges merely "interpret" rather than create law has been thoroughly debunked by legal scholars across the political spectrum. Constitutional text is often vague, and its application to modern controversies requires choices that are inherently political. When the Court decides whether "liberty" includes reproductive rights, or whether "equal protection" prohibits affirmative action, it makes policy decisions indistinguishable from legislative choices—except these decisions cannot be reversed through normal democratic processes.

Historical Illegitimacy of Judicial Review

Absent from the Constitutional Text

The Constitution nowhere explicitly grants federal courts the power to invalidate legislation. Article III establishes the judicial branch but limits its role to deciding "cases" and "controversies." The Founders, who specified powers in meticulous detail elsewhere, would surely have explicitly stated such an momentous authority had they intended courts to possess it.

A Self-Appointed Power

Founders' Intent

Many Founders explicitly rejected judicial supremacy. Thomas Jefferson warned that judicial review would make the Constitution "a mere thing of wax in the hands of the judiciary." James Madison, the Constitution's primary architect, believed each branch had equal authority to interpret the Constitution within its sphere. The current system betrays these democratic insights.

The Harms of Judicial Supremacy

Policy Stagnation

The Court's anti-democratic interventions have repeatedly blocked necessary social and economic reforms. From striking down New Deal legislation during the Depression to gutting campaign finance reform in Citizens United, the Court has consistently favored entrenched interests over democratic change. Judicial review creates an insurmountable barrier to progress, requiring constitutional amendments—nearly impossible in our polarized age—to overcome judicial vetoes of popular legislation.

This reality corrodes the rule of law itself, as citizens correctly perceive the Court as just another political institution, but one uniquely insulated from democratic accountability.

Legislative Constitutional Interpretation

Congress and state legislatures should reclaim their co-equal role in constitutional interpretation. Elected representatives, accountable to voters, should determine whether proposed legislation comports with constitutional principles. This would force legislators to take their constitutional oaths seriously and defend their interpretations to constituents.

Popular Constitutional Review

For particularly significant constitutional questions, direct democracy could play a role. National referenda on constitutional interpretation would give the people themselves—the ultimate sovereigns in a democracy—final say over their fundamental law. This could be implemented through a system where congressional constitutional interpretations could be challenged via petition and resolved by popular vote.

Supermajority Override

Critics argue judicial review protects vulnerable minorities from majority tyranny. However, history shows the Court has more often been an obstacle to minority rights than their champion. From Dred Scott to Plessy v. Ferguson to gutting the Voting Rights Act, the Court has consistently sided with powerful interests against the vulnerable. Democratic deliberation about constitutional meaning would enhance, not diminish, constitutional understanding.

The Supreme Court and judicial review represent an autocratic anomaly in what claims to be a democratic republic. Nine unelected lawyers should not possess unreviewable power to shape society according to their preferences. Constitutional interpretation belongs to the people, exercised through their elected representatives or directly through democratic participation.

Abolishing the Supreme Court and judicial review would not mean abandoning constitutionalism—it would mean taking it seriously as a democratic practice rather than an elite imposition. A constitution that truly belongs to the people must be interpreted by the people. Only then can we claim to live in a genuine democracy where popular sovereignty is more than rhetoric.

The path forward requires courage to challenge entrenched institutions and reclaim the revolutionary spirit of democratic self-governance. For those who believe in democracy not merely as a procedure but as a fundamental principle of legitimate governance, the conclusion is inescapable—the Supreme Court and judicial review must go.

Introduction
The United States Supreme Court stands as one of the most powerful judicial bodies in the world. This potent mechanism, largely established by the famous 1803 case Marbury v. Madison, has enshrined an unelected group of nine justices as the ultimate arbiters of constitutional meaning. While the system was originally designed to safeguard minority rights and ensure government adherence to fundamental law, it increasingly circumvents democratic processes. This essay makes the case for abolishing the Supreme Court in its current form and eliminating judicial review, instead entrusting matters of constitutional interpretation to elected representatives or direct popular vote.

I. Concentration of Power and Lack of Democratic Accountability
A. Unelected Decision-Makers
Supreme Court justices are appointed, not elected, and serve lifetime terms. This arrangement effectively removes them from meaningful accountability. They wield extraordinary influence, shaping legal and social policy for generations. An institution so insulated from the electorate runs contrary to the democratic ideal: the notion that power should flow from the people and reflect their evolving values.

B. Constitutional Interpretation Beyond the People’s Reach
Although the Constitution can be amended, the amendment process is exceedingly cumbersome. As a result, rulings by the Supreme Court often feel final and nearly impossible for ordinary citizens to overturn. Decisions handed down by nine unelected officials act as de facto constitutional amendments, regardless of shifts in public opinion or changes in elected leadership.

C. Lack of Direct Public Input
When the nation’s highest court rules on issues like reproductive health, voting law, or civil rights, there is no direct path for the electorate to challenge such decisions swiftly. Citizens are coerced into acceptance, even if a majority disagrees, until a new case or a rare constitutional amendment emerges. This dynamic limits the electorate’s agency and can stifle national consensus-building.

II. Historic Flaws and Ideological Swings
A. Inconsistency Over Time
Supreme Court rulings have varied drastically as the Court’s makeup changes. The notion that a fundamental constitutional principle can depend on the personal leanings of a handful of justices undermines faith in the legal system. The back-and-forth swings on pivotal issues—ranging from segregation and civil rights to campaign finance—reflect ideological oscillations that thwart consistency and predictability in the law.

B. Past Errors with Lasting Consequences
Throughout its history, the Supreme Court has issued decisions that contemporary Americans widely denounce. Cases like Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857) and Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) highlight that the Court is not inherently more enlightened than elected branches. By placing constitutional interpretation in the hands of the people and their representatives, society is better able to correct missteps in real time instead of waiting decades for jurisprudential shifts.

III. Strengthening Democracy through Elected Oversight
A. Empowering the Legislature—Voice of the People
Transferring constitutional interpretation to Congress could ensure that decisions rest with individuals directly accountable to constituents. Representatives, who face elections on a regular basis, would be more in tune with public sentiment. If a large swath of the population disagrees with a particular constitutional interpretation, they can vote their representatives out and replace them with new ones who better align with their principles.

B. Public Discourse and Direct Voting
In especially contentious areas of constitutional law, direct popular votes could supplement or replace legislative interpretations. Whether through nationwide referendums or carefully structured ballot initiatives, entrusting citizens with final say on vital constitutional questions fosters widespread civic engagement. It also reaffirms the founding democratic principle that ultimate power resides in “We the People,” not in a lifetime-appointed judiciary.

C. Flexibility and Adaptability
By removing judicial review and replacing it with a democratic system of checks and balances, constitutional interpretation can evolve with society. Instead of waiting for court cases to wind their way through the legal system, the electorate and its representatives can respond more swiftly and transparently. This agility would prove invaluable in addressing modern challenges—such as technological privacy rights or environmental protections—that demand nuanced, timely decision-making.

IV. Addressing Potential Criticisms
A. Risk of Majoritarian Tyranny
A common argument supporting a strong Supreme Court is that it protects minority rights from majoritarian overreach. However, robust legislative mechanisms, independent administrative bodies, and clearly enshrined civil rights protections can safeguard minorities without resorting to an unaccountable, permanent judicial branch. Systems of checks and balances involving multiple democratic institutions—coupled with legal protections in statutory law—can be more responsive and protective than a narrow group of justices.

B. Complexity and Feasibility
Abolishing the Supreme Court and removing judicial review is undoubtedly a monumental endeavor. Critics may argue it would undermine stability and clarity. Yet no system is beyond reform. Just as the Constitution itself has been amended, the nation can replace an unresponsive judiciary with a reimagined structure that directly involves lawmakers and citizens. Over time, citizens and their representatives would develop new traditions, precedents, and procedures that match democratic values and modern realities.

C. Value of Expertise and Precedent
Opponents also rightly note that justices bring legal expertise and can weigh technical arguments impartially. These benefits need not vanish if the Supreme Court is dissolved. Conclusion
The United States prides itself on being a government “of the people, by the people, for the people,” yet the Supreme Court and the principle of judicial review vest ultimate constitutional authority in a small, unelected body. The Court’s historical mistakes, ideological pendulum swings, and lack of direct accountability to the electorate challenge the nation’s democratic foundations. By abolishing the Supreme Court and ending judicial review, America can distribute the power of constitutional interpretation more broadly among those elected to serve the public—whether through legislative decision-making or direct popular votes. Such a transition would not be simple; it would demand robust new checks and balances, enhanced protections for minority rights, and new legal mechanisms to guide complex questions. The People's Constitution: A Case for Abolishing the Supreme Court and Restoring Popular Sovereignty

The United States Constitution begins with a powerful, revolutionary phrase: “We the People.” This foundational principle of popular sovereignty—that the ultimate source of governmental authority is the consent of the governed—is the bedrock of American democracy. Yet, for over two centuries, this principle has been subtly and profoundly undermined by an unelected, unaccountable judicial body: the Supreme Court of the United States. Through its self-claimed power of judicial review—the authority to strike down laws passed by elected representatives—the Court has become a super-legislature, insulating contentious social and political debates from the democratic process. To reclaim the promise of a government of, by, and for the people, it is not enough to reform the Court; we must abolish it outright and eliminate the anti-democratic principle of judicial review, vesting the ultimate power of constitutional interpretation where it belongs: with the people and their elected representatives.

The most potent argument for abolition is the fundamental illegitimacy of judicial review itself. Nowhere in the Constitution is the Supreme Court explicitly granted the power to nullify acts of Congress. This authority was seized by the Court itself in the 1803 case of Marbury v. Madison. In a brilliant act of political judo, Chief Justice John Marshall established the precedent, creating a power that has grown to dwarf that of the other branches. This is a profound democratic deficit. Nine individuals, appointed for life and answerable to no electorate, can single-handedly override the will of millions of citizens expressed through their representatives in Congress and the President. This system transforms the Constitution from a living document, adaptable through amendment and legislative practice, into a rigid text whose meaning is locked behind the doors of a judicial monastery. On issues from campaign finance and voting rights to healthcare and civil liberties, a handful of lawyers in robes can dictate national policy, rendering the arduous, democratic work of campaigning, legislating, and consensus-building moot with a single 5-4 decision.

Furthermore, the modern confirmation process has exposed the Court not as a neutral arbiter of law, but as a deeply political and partisan institution. The spectacle of highly-charged Senate hearings, where nominees perform rhetorical gymnastics to avoid revealing their true beliefs, is a farcical performance masking a raw power struggle. Justices are increasingly selected not for their jurisprudential wisdom but for their perceived ideological allegiance, turning the Court into a proxy war for the political branches. The result is a body whose credibility is in tatters, viewed by the public not as an impartial institution but as an extension of the party that appointed its majority. Landmark decisions are increasingly seen not as settled law but as temporary victories awaiting the next judicial appointment. This politicization erodes public trust in the rule of law itself and creates a volatile legal environment where fundamental rights can be granted and rescinded not by the people, but by the timing of a justice’s retirement or death.

Critics will argue that an independent judiciary is essential to protect minority rights from the “tyranny of the majority.” This is the most common, yet most overstated, defense of the Court’s power. History reveals that the Court has more often been an impediment to justice than a protector of it. It was the Supreme Court that affirmed the property rights of slaveholders in Dred Scott v. Sandford, that sanctioned racial segregation in Plessy v. Ferguson, and that upheld the internment of Japanese Americans in Korematsu v. United States. Progress on civil rights was achieved not primarily through judicial decree, but through the painful, democratic struggles of social movements that forced elected representatives to pass transformative legislation like the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965. The true safeguard for minority rights in a democracy is not judicial fiat, but a robust culture of civil liberties, a free press, and a political system designed to build broad, inclusive coalitions. Rights secured through democratic persuasion and legislation are far more durable and legitimate than those granted by judicial elites, which are perpetually vulnerable to being overturned by the next judicial cohort.

Therefore, we must envision and advocate for a new system. Abolishing the Supreme Court does not mean abandoning constitutional government. It means reinventing it. The power of constitutional interpretation should be returned to the elected branches of government. Congress, as the most directly representative body, would have the primary responsibility for ensuring its laws are constitutional. Disagreements between Congress and the President could be resolved through political negotiation and electoral accountability, not judicial arbitration. This system, often called “departmentalism” or “coordinate construction,” was supported by figures like Thomas Jefferson and Abraham Lincoln, who believed each branch had a duty to interpret the Constitution within its own sphere.

To further empower popular sovereignty, we should lower the barriers for passing constitutional amendments, making the document easier for the people to update directly. More radically, we could adopt a version of the Swiss model, where certain fundamental constitutional changes are decided by national referendum. This would force a genuine national conversation on profound issues, educating the citizenry and building a more engaged and responsible electorate. Imagine the national discourse that would occur if the rights to privacy, bear arms, or free speech were debated in town halls and living rooms across the country, rather than in the cloistered confines of the Supreme Court. The result would be a constitution that truly reflects the evolving conscience of the nation, not the frozen preferences of a bygone era interpreted through a modern ideological lens.

The current system of judicial supremacy is a historical anomaly and a democratic failure. It has centralized immense power in an unaccountable institution, stifled political debate, and fostered public cynicism. The courage to abolish the Supreme Court and end judicial review is not an attack on the Constitution, but its ultimate fulfillment. It is a demand to realize the radical promise of self-governance enshrined in the Declaration of Independence and the first three words of our Constitution. It is time to dissolve the judicial oligarchy and trust “We the People” to be the final arbiters of our own destiny. Let us have the confidence in our democratic principles to reclaim our Constitution and build a more perfect, and more democratic, union.
