The Case for Democratic Constitutional Interpretation: Why America Should Abolish the Supreme Court

A Persuasive Essay

Introduction

In 1803, Chief Justice John Marshall, in a breathtaking act of institutional self-empowerment, declared in Marbury v. Madison that the Supreme Court possessed the authority to strike down laws passed by the people's representatives. Nowhere in the Constitution is this power explicitly granted. In the more than two centuries since, nine unelected individuals — appointed for life, accountable to no voter, removable by virtually no practical mechanism — have shaped American society more profoundly than perhaps any other institution. They have decided who counts as a person, who can marry whom, what the police can do to your body, and whether your vote matters equally. The question Americans have been trained never to ask is simple: Why should they?

The United States Supreme Court, and the broader principle of judicial review it embodies, represents the single greatest structural contradiction in American democracy. It is time to abolish it and return constitutional interpretation to where democratic theory demands it reside — with the people themselves, through their elected representatives and, on fundamental questions, through direct popular vote.

I. The Anti-Democratic Foundation

The argument for abolition begins with an uncomfortable truth: judicial review is, at its core, an anti-democratic institution dressed in constitutional clothing.

Consider the basic arithmetic of the current system. Five people — a bare majority of the nine-member Court — can invalidate legislation supported by majorities in the House of Representatives, the Senate, and signed by the President. Five people can overturn the expressed will of hundreds of millions. These five people were not elected. They do not face reelection. They serve for life. They can be removed only through impeachment, a mechanism so cumbersome it has never successfully removed a Supreme Court Justice in American history.

Defenders of the Court will immediately object that democracy requires constraints — that majority rule unchecked becomes tyranny. This is true but irrelevant to the structural question. The issue is not whether constitutional constraints should exist, but who interprets them. There is no inherent reason why interpretation must rest with unelected judges rather than with the democratic process itself. Many functioning democracies operate with far weaker forms of judicial review or none at all. The Netherlands, for example, explicitly prohibits courts from reviewing the constitutionality of legislation. New Zealand and the United Kingdom have historically operated without American-style judicial supremacy. Switzerland regularly puts constitutional questions to popular referendum. These nations have not descended into tyranny. In many global indices of freedom, equality, and human rights, they outperform the United States.

The philosopher Jeremy Waldron has made the most rigorous contemporary case against judicial review, arguing that among people who take rights seriously but disagree about their application, there is no reason to privilege the moral reasoning of judges over that of legislators or citizens. Disagreement about rights is not a sign of democratic failure — it is the permanent condition of a pluralistic society. The question is always procedural: who gets to decide? Democracy answers: the people. Judicial review answers: the judges. One must choose.

II. The Myth of Apolitical Jurisprudence

The Supreme Court's legitimacy rests on a carefully cultivated myth — that Justices are not political actors but neutral interpreters applying law through reason and expertise. This myth has always been fiction, and in the contemporary era, it has become transparently so.

Every major constitutional provision that the Court regularly interprets — "equal protection," "due process," "cruel and unusual punishment," "unreasonable searches," the "establishment" of religion — is written in language of profound generality. These phrases do not interpret themselves. Their application to specific controversies requires value choices, and value choices are, by definition, political. When the Court decides whether the Second Amendment protects individual gun ownership or whether the Fourteenth Amendment encompasses a right to abortion, it is not discovering pre-existing legal truths. It is making policy judgments — the same kind of judgments legislators make, except without democratic accountability.

The confirmation process has made this reality undeniable. If Supreme Court appointments were genuinely about legal expertise rather than ideology, confirmation hearings would not be the partisan battlefields they have become. Presidents would not construct shortlists based on predicted voting patterns. Senators would not vote almost exclusively along party lines. Interest groups would not spend millions of dollars lobbying for or against nominees. Everyone involved in the process — the President, the Senate, advocacy organizations, the media, and the public — understands that appointing a Justice is appointing a policymaker. The only people who maintain the pretense otherwise are the Justices themselves.

The historical record confirms this. The Court that decided Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857) was not applying neutral principles when it declared Black people could never be citizens — it was imposing the slaveholding ideology of its majority. The Court that decided Lochner v. New York (1905) was not engaging in dispassionate constitutional analysis when it struck down labor regulations — it was encoding laissez-faire economics into constitutional law. The Court that decided Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) was not faithfully interpreting the Fourteenth Amendment when it upheld racial segregation — it was ratifying white supremacy. In each case, the Court exercised raw political power while claiming merely to follow the law.

If constitutional interpretation is inevitably political, then democratic principles demand that it be performed by political actors who are accountable to the people. There is no justification for a system in which the most consequential political decisions in American life are made by officials who face no electoral consequences whatsoever.

III. The Counter-Majoritarian Difficulty Is Not a Feature — It Is a Bug

The standard defense of judicial review is that it protects minority rights against majority tyranny. This narrative, taught in every civics class and law school in America, is more mythology than history.

For most of its existence, the Supreme Court has used its counter-majoritarian power not to protect vulnerable minorities but to protect powerful minorities — slaveholders, corporations, and entrenched economic interests — against democratic majorities seeking progressive reform.

The historical ledger is damning. Before the Warren Court era (1953–1969), the Supreme Court's most consequential exercises of judicial review included: protecting slavery (Dred Scott), invalidating the income tax (Pollock v. Farmers' Loan & Trust Co.), gutting Reconstruction-era civil rights legislation (The Civil Rights Cases), upholding segregation (Plessy), striking down child labor laws (Hammer v. Dagenhart), and systematically dismantling New Deal economic legislation during the 1930s. For roughly 150 years, judicial review was predominantly a tool of reaction, wielded against the interests of workers, racial minorities, and the poor.

The Warren Court represents roughly fifteen years in which the Court moved ahead of democratic majorities on civil rights and civil liberties. Even here, the narrative is more complex than conventionally presented. Brown v. Board of Education (1954) is the crown jewel of the judicial review defense, yet scholars like Gerald Rosenberg have demonstrated in rigorous empirical work (The Hollow Hope) that Brown produced almost no actual school desegregation for over a decade. Real desegregation came from the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the enforcement mechanisms of the elected branches. The democratic process, once mobilized, accomplished what the Court could not.

Moreover, for every Brown, there is a Shelby County v. Holder (2013), in which the Court gutted the Voting Rights Act — one of the most important pieces of civil rights legislation in American history — over the objections of overwhelming Congressional majorities who had reauthorized it. For every Obergefell v. Hodges (2015), there is a Citizens United v. FEC (2010), in which the Court overrode democratic attempts to regulate the corrupting influence of money in politics. The Court gives with one hand and takes with the other, and there is no mechanism by which the people can predict or control which hand will move.

The deeper problem is structural. Even if one believed that the Warren Court era vindicated judicial review, one would have to explain why the mechanism for protecting minority rights should be one that, for the vast majority of American history, has done the opposite. A slot machine that occasionally pays out does not become a sound investment strategy. A system of rights protection that works only when the right people happen to be appointed — and fails catastrophically otherwise — is not a system at all. It is a gamble.

IV. Life Tenure and the Gerontocratic Problem

The Constitution provides that federal judges "shall hold their Offices during good Behaviour" — effectively guaranteeing life tenure. When the Constitution was ratified, average life expectancy was approximately 35-40 years, and Justices served an average of roughly 15 years. Today, Justices routinely serve 25-35 years. The result is a system in which individuals appointed in one political era continue to shape constitutional law for decades, long after the political coalition that appointed them has dissolved and the social conditions that shaped their worldview have transformed beyond recognition.

Justice Clarence Thomas, appointed in 1991, continues to shape constitutional interpretation more than three decades later. If he serves to a comparable age as several of his predecessors, he could serve into the 2030s — meaning that a single unelected individual would have influenced American constitutional law for nearly half a century. No President serves that long. No Senator serves with that degree of unaccountable power. In no other functioning democracy do jurists wield such enduring, unchecked authority.

Life tenure creates perverse strategic incentives. Justices time their retirements to ensure ideologically compatible successors. Presidents seek to appoint young nominees to maximize their appointee's tenure. The death or incapacitation of a single Justice — as the nation witnessed with Justice Scalia's death in 2016 and Justice Ginsburg's death in 2020 — creates constitutional crises in which the ideological direction of the Court turns on biological accident. This is not a system designed by political genius. It is a system held together by luck and actuarial tables.

Abolishing the Court eliminates the life tenure problem entirely. Constitutional interpretation by elected representatives ensures regular democratic renewal. Interpretation by popular vote ensures direct accountability. Neither system requires the nation to hold its collective breath every time an octogenarian Justice is hospitalized.

V. The Proposed Alternative: Democratic Constitutional Interpretation

Abolition of the Supreme Court need not mean abolition of constitutionalism. The Constitution would remain the supreme law of the land. What would change is the mechanism of interpretation. Several models deserve consideration.

Legislative Constitutional Interpretation. Under this model, Congress would bear primary responsibility for interpreting the Constitution, as many framers originally expected. When legislation is challenged as unconstitutional, the question would be resolved through the legislative process — committee hearings, debate, and vote. This system has the virtue of transparency: legislators must publicly justify their constitutional reasoning and face electoral consequences for their interpretive choices. Unlike Justices who serve for life and write opinions that most Americans never read, legislators operate in the open and answer to voters.

This approach has strong historical pedigree. In the early Republic, "departmentalism" — the view that each branch of government has co-equal authority to interpret the Constitution — was a mainstream position held by Jefferson, Jackson, and Lincoln, among others. Lincoln explicitly rejected the idea that the Supreme Court's interpretation of the Constitution was binding on the other branches, arguing in his First Inaugural Address that if "the policy of the Government upon vital questions affecting the whole people is to be irrevocably fixed by decisions of the Supreme Court," then "the people will have ceased to be their own rulers."

Popular Constitutional Referenda. For the most fundamental constitutional questions — the scope of individual rights, the limits of government power, the meaning of equality — the people themselves should decide through direct vote. Switzerland has successfully used constitutional referenda for over 150 years. When Swiss citizens disagree about constitutional meaning, they vote. The result is a constitutional culture in which citizens are actively engaged in constitutional interpretation rather than passively waiting for nine appointed elders to hand down rulings.

Critics will argue that popular majorities cannot be trusted with rights questions. But this argument proves too much. If the people cannot be trusted to interpret their own Constitution, they cannot be trusted to elect the officials who appoint and confirm the Justices who currently interpret it. The entire democratic enterprise rests on the premise that ordinary citizens possess sufficient wisdom to govern themselves. Judicial review is a vote of no confidence in that premise.

A Hybrid Model. The most practical approach would likely combine elements of both systems. Congress would serve as the primary interpreter of constitutional provisions in the course of ordinary legislation, with a supermajority requirement (perhaps two-thirds) for interpreting provisions that restrict individual rights. On questions of fundamental rights, citizens could trigger a constitutional referendum through petition, ensuring that the most consequential decisions receive direct democratic input.

Constitutional advisory panels composed of legal scholars, retired legislators, and citizen representatives could provide non-binding interpretive guidance, ensuring that democratic constitutional interpretation benefits from expertise without being controlled by it.

VI. Answering the Objections

"The tyranny of the majority will trample minority rights."

This is the strongest objection, and it deserves a serious response. First, as demonstrated above, the historical record shows that the Court has more frequently been a tool of majority oppression than a shield against it. Second, structural constitutional protections — federalism, separation of powers, bicameralism, the Bill of Rights as interpreted through democratic processes — provide significant protections against majoritarian excess without requiring judicial supremacy. Third, international evidence demonstrates that democracies without strong judicial review (the UK, New Zealand, the Netherlands, the Scandinavian countries) consistently perform as well as or better than the United States on measures of minority rights protection, civil liberties, and human freedom. The Court is not the only, or even the most effective, mechanism for protecting rights. Democratic culture, civic education, a free press, and robust civil society institutions may matter far more.

"Elected officials lack legal expertise."

Constitutional interpretation is not, as argued above, primarily a technical legal exercise. It is a political and moral exercise. To the extent that legal expertise is valuable, it can be provided through advisory mechanisms without granting lawyers unelected veto power over democratic decisions. Congress already employs extensive legal staff. Executive agencies include armies of constitutional lawyers. The expertise exists within the democratic system; it simply needs to serve democracy rather than override it.

"This would require a constitutional amendment and is therefore impractical."

Practicality and principle are different questions. The abolition of slavery also required a constitutional amendment. Women's suffrage required a constitutional amendment. The question is whether the principle is sound. If it is, the practical obstacles — while real — become challenges to be overcome rather than reasons for surrender. Moreover, certain versions of this proposal could be implemented without formal amendment. Congress possesses the constitutional power to strip the Court of appellate jurisdiction under Article III. Congress controls the Court's budget and size. A determined Congress could effectively curtail judicial review through existing constitutional mechanisms while building support for a formal amendment.

"What about Brown v. Board of Education?"

Brown is the emotional trump card played in every defense of judicial review. It should be acknowledged as a genuine achievement. But one case — or even a handful of cases — cannot justify an entire institutional structure. If Brown is the strongest argument for judicial review, it must be weighed against Dred Scott, Plessy, Lochner, Korematsu (upholding Japanese internment), Bush v. Gore, Citizens United, and Shelby County. When the full ledger is examined, the Court's record on justice is, at best, mixed. Moreover, as noted earlier, Brown's actual impact was minimal until the democratic branches acted. The lesson of the civil rights movement is not that courts saved democracy — it is that democratic mobilization succeeded where courts alone could not.

VII. Constitutional Fidelity and Democratic Self-Governance

At the deepest level, the argument for abolishing the Supreme Court is an argument about what kind of society America wants to be. The Constitution opens with "We the People" — not "We the Justices" or "We the Lawyers." It establishes a system of self-governance in which the people, through their representatives, make the fundamental decisions that shape their collective life. Judicial review takes the most important of those decisions — questions of rights, liberty, equality, and the structure of government — and hands them to a tiny, unelected, unaccountable elite.

This arrangement might be justified if the elite consistently produced just outcomes. It does not. It might be justified if constitutional interpretation were a technical exercise beyond the competence of ordinary citizens. It is not. It might be justified if no alternative existed. Alternatives abound.

The American people have been taught to revere the Supreme Court as the guardian of their liberties. In reality, they are capable of guarding their own liberties — and have done so, repeatedly, through democratic mobilization, constitutional amendment, and legislative action. The Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery not through judicial review but through democratic will enforced by war. The Nineteenth Amendment enfranchised women not through judicial decree but through decades of democratic organizing. The Civil Rights Act of 1964 transformed American society not because the Court commanded it but because the people demanded it.

The Supreme Court did not give Americans their rights. Americans claimed their rights through democratic struggle. It is time to build a constitutional system that reflects this reality — a system in which the people are not supplicants before a judicial throne but the ultimate interpreters of their own Constitution.

Conclusion

Abolishing the Supreme Court would be the most significant structural reform in American history since the ratification of the Constitution itself. It would be disorienting. It would be fiercely contested. It would require Americans to take ownership of constitutional questions they have long been content to outsource to nine robed figures in a marble temple.

But it would also represent the fulfillment of a democratic promise that has been deferred for over two centuries. It would end the charade that constitutional law is apolitical. It would eliminate the grotesque spectacle of confirmation battles that treat Supreme Court seats as ideological prizes. It would remove the dead hand of life-tenured Justices from the nation's most vital policy debates. And it would affirm, finally and irrevocably, that in a democracy, the people rule — not just in electing their representatives, but in interpreting the fundamental law that governs them all.

The Supreme Court was never the last safeguard of American liberty. The American people were. It is time the constitutional order recognized what history has long demonstrated.

Note: This essay was written as a persuasive exercise presenting one side of a complex constitutional debate. The arguments for judicial review and an independent judiciary — including protection of minority rights, institutional stability, legal consistency, and insulation of fundamental rights from political passions — are substantial and widely held. A complete assessment of this question requires serious engagement with both sides.

It is time to complete the democratic revolution that our founders began. They built a republic — imperfect, aspirational, evolving. They did not build a kritarchy — a government by judges. That came later, incrementally, by accretion and acquiescence.
